soc2.name: AICPA Trust Services Criteria (SOC 2)
soc2.official_citation: TSP Section 100 — 2017 Trust Services Criteria for Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy (With Revised Points of Focus — 2022)
soc2.scope: Service organization controls audit framework. Common criteria CC1-CC5 align to the 17 COSO Internal Control — Integrated Framework principles. Common criteria CC6-CC9 are supplemental criteria for logical/physical access, system operations, change management, and risk mitigation. Category-specific criteria for Availability (A series), Processing Integrity (PI series), Confidentiality (C series), and Privacy (P series) supplement the common criteria.
soc2.source: AICPA — TSP Section 100, distributed at https://www.aicpa-cima.com/resources/download/2017-trust-services-criteria-with-revised-points-of-focus-2022 (registration-gated public download).
soc2.verified_against: Local PDF of TSP Section 100 (cover page identifies it as the AICPA-published 2017 Trust Services Criteria with Revised Points of Focus — 2022). All sub-criterion titles below were verbatim-extracted from pages 14-50 of that document on 2026-05-10.

common_criteria_subcriteria.CC1.1: COSO Principle 1: The entity demonstrates a commitment to integrity and ethical values.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC1.2: COSO Principle 2: The board of directors demonstrates independence from management and exercises oversight of the development and performance of internal control.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC1.3: COSO Principle 3: Management establishes, with board oversight, structures, reporting lines, and appropriate authorities and responsibilities in the pursuit of objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC1.4: COSO Principle 4: The entity demonstrates a commitment to attract, develop, and retain competent individuals in alignment with objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC1.5: COSO Principle 5: The entity holds individuals accountable for their internal control responsibilities in the pursuit of objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC2.1: COSO Principle 13: The entity obtains or generates and uses relevant, quality information to support the functioning of internal control.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC2.2: COSO Principle 14: The entity internally communicates information, including objectives and responsibilities for internal control, necessary to support the functioning of internal control.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC2.3: COSO Principle 15: The entity communicates with external parties regarding matters affecting the functioning of internal control.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC3.1: COSO Principle 6: The entity specifies objectives with sufficient clarity to enable the identification and assessment of risks relating to objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC3.2: COSO Principle 7: The entity identifies risks to the achievement of its objectives across the entity and analyzes risks as a basis for determining how the risks should be managed.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC3.3: COSO Principle 8: The entity considers the potential for fraud in assessing risks to the achievement of objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC3.4: COSO Principle 9: The entity identifies and assesses changes that could significantly impact the system of internal control.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC4.1: COSO Principle 16: The entity selects, develops, and performs ongoing and/or separate evaluations to ascertain whether the components of internal control are present and functioning.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC4.2: COSO Principle 17: The entity evaluates and communicates internal control deficiencies in a timely manner to those parties responsible for taking corrective action, including senior management and the board of directors, as appropriate.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC5.1: COSO Principle 10: The entity selects and develops control activities that contribute to the mitigation of risks to the achievement of objectives to acceptable levels.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC5.2: COSO Principle 11: The entity also selects and develops general control activities over technology to support the achievement of objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC5.3: COSO Principle 12: The entity deploys control activities through policies that establish what is expected and in procedures that put policies into action.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC6.1: The entity implements logical access security software, infrastructure, and architectures over protected information assets to protect them from security events to meet the entity's objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC6.2: Prior to issuing system credentials and granting system access, the entity registers and authorizes new internal and external users whose access is administered by the entity. For those users whose access is administered by the entity, user system credentials are removed when user access is no longer authorized.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC6.3: The entity authorizes, modifies, or removes access to data, software, functions, and other protected information assets based on roles, responsibilities, or the system design and changes, giving consideration to the concepts of least privilege and segregation of duties, to meet the entity's objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC6.4: The entity restricts physical access to facilities and protected information assets (for example, data center facilities, backup media storage, and other sensitive locations) to authorized personnel to meet the entity's objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC6.5: The entity discontinues logical and physical protections over physical assets only after the ability to read or recover data and software from those assets has been diminished and is no longer required to meet the entity's objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC6.6: The entity implements logical access security measures to protect against threats from sources outside its system boundaries.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC6.7: The entity restricts the transmission, movement, and removal of information to authorized internal and external users and processes, and protects it during transmission, movement, or removal to meet the entity's objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC6.8: The entity implements controls to prevent or detect and act upon the introduction of unauthorized or malicious software to meet the entity's objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC7.1: To meet its objectives, the entity uses detection and monitoring procedures to identify (1) changes to configurations that result in the introduction of new vulnerabilities, and (2) susceptibilities to newly discovered vulnerabilities.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC7.2: The entity monitors system components and the operation of those components for anomalies that are indicative of malicious acts, natural disasters, and errors affecting the entity's ability to meet its objectives; anomalies are analyzed to determine whether they represent security events.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC7.3: The entity evaluates security events to determine whether they could or have resulted in a failure of the entity to meet its objectives (security incidents) and, if so, takes actions to prevent or address such failures.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC7.4: The entity responds to identified security incidents by executing a defined incident-response program to understand, contain, remediate, and communicate security incidents, as appropriate.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC7.5: The entity identifies, develops, and implements activities to recover from identified security incidents.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC8.1: The entity authorizes, designs, develops or acquires, configures, documents, tests, approves, and implements changes to infrastructure, data, software, and procedures to meet its objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC9.1: The entity identifies, selects, and develops risk mitigation activities for risks arising from potential business disruptions.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC9.2: The entity assesses and manages risks associated with vendors and business partners.

Permit logs every authorized invocation of the AI-enabled service. Does not prevent abuse via the legitimate product surface, but provides forensic evidence of usage patterns.

binding_request_hash binds the canonical wire body at dispatch — post-decision request alteration (one class of prompt injection) is cryptographically detectable. Does not prevent prompt-injection at the input layer; provides evidence chain of what was authorized vs what was dispatched.

Every agent tool invocation requires a Permit. action_name identifies the tool; actions_json captures parameters; subject_id binds the invoking agent. Constraints/budgets prevent escalation via legitimate tools.

control_mappings.permit_evidence: Every Permit decision is an event log entry. Permit substrate captures ALL AI-decision events emitted; AU-2 organization-defined-list of events is satisfied at the AI-action boundary.

Permit decision_details + closure_v2 capture: what type of event occurred (action_name), when (created_at + TSA timestamp), where (resource_provider + resource_model), source (subject_id + project_id), outcome (decision: allow/deny/challenge), identity (subject_id), and additional context (policy_id + policy_version). Exceeds AU-3 minimum content requirements for the AI-action surface.

Keel tier policies set retention windows: Starter 7d, Production 180d, Enterprise 365d. External R2 checkpoint anchoring offloads checkpoint storage from primary tenant. Audit-log storage capacity assessment is the customer's responsibility under their boundary; Keel provides documented retention floors.

control_mappings.control_title: Audit Record Reduction and Report Generation
control_mappings.permit_evidence: Audit export bundle is queryable and content-addressed via manifest. Customer integrates Keel exports with their reporting workflows. Permit substrate provides the records; reduction/report generation lives in the customer's reporting layer.

Every Permit carries created_at server timestamp. Enterprise-tier integration with RFC 3161 Time-Stamp Authority (FreeTSA.org default, or any RFC 3161 TSA) provides independent third-party time witness on integrity checkpoints. TSA receipts bind the audit chain state to externally verifiable time, exceeding AU-8 'organization-defined granularity' for AI-action timestamps.

Per-project hash chain prevents tampering with audit records (each record cryptographically bound to predecessor via SHA-256). Ed25519 signed exports prevent post-export tampering. AU-9 'protect audit information and audit logging tools from unauthorized access, modification, and deletion' is satisfied via cryptographic primitives, not just access controls.

control_mappings.control_title: Protection of Audit Information | Store on Separate Physical Systems or Components
control_mappings.permit_evidence: External checkpoint anchoring publishes signed chain snapshots to S3-compatible storage (Cloudflare R2 by default, or customer-controlled bucket) every 5 minutes via cron. Checkpoints are byte-identical to primary chain state but stored on infrastructure separate from the Keel service. Satisfies AU-9(2) 'store audit logs on a different system' for the Permit substrate.

control_mappings.control_title: Protection of Audit Information | Cryptographic Protection
control_mappings.permit_evidence: Hash chain (SHA-256), Ed25519 signed exports, RFC 3161 TSA receipts. Three cryptographic protection mechanisms layered: chain integrity, export authenticity, and time-witnessing. AU-9(3) 'implement cryptographic mechanisms to protect the integrity of audit information' is satisfied with named, auditable primitives.

Ed25519 signed exports bind audit content to a specific signing key under Keel's control. Signing key rotation history (migration 0146) preserves verification across key rotations via active-windows in the public manifest. RFC 3161 TSA receipts add independent time witness. Customer's verifier CLI reproduces signature verification without Keel-side access. AU-10 non-repudiation is satisfied for the AI-action surface.

Production 180d retention exceeds EU AI Act Art 26(6) ≥6mo floor. Enterprise 365d retention. Retention is plan-tier-gated and enforced at the database layer (RLS-protected). Customer should specify their organization-defined retention period and select Keel tier accordingly; for FedRAMP-typical 3-year audit retention, Enterprise tier + customer-side archive of monthly signed exports is the supported pattern.

Permit primitive IS the audit record generation mechanism for AI-action events. Hash chain ensures records cannot be silently dropped (chain continuity is verifiable). Every Permit produces a record; record generation cannot be selectively bypassed without breaking chain verification.

Permit is the AI-action access enforcement mechanism. policy_id + policy_version stamp the enforcement rule; subject_id binds the requesting identity. Denied permits log unauthorized-access attempts. Note: AC-3 covers system access broadly; Permit enforces at the AI-action boundary only — system-level access enforcement remains customer responsibility.

policy_id + policy_version stamped on every Permit binds each AI decision to a specific configuration version. Necessary for customer demonstrating CM-3 compliance for AI policy changes; not sufficient for general system configuration change control.

resource_provider + resource_model on every Permit forms a queryable inventory of AI components used (which providers, which models). Supports the AI portion of system component inventory. Customer responsible for general system component inventory beyond AI components.

Per-project hash chain emits continuous audit evidence. External checkpoint cadence (every 5 minutes) provides ongoing integrity proof. Replay drift detection identifies behavioral changes over time. Provides the AI-action telemetry for the customer's continuous monitoring program.

Incident evidence export bundle (shipped 2026-04-25) packages signed evidence for incident response workflows. Tampering detection codes (WALK_RECORD_HASH_MISMATCH, WALK_CLOSURE_DISPATCH_DIGEST_MISMATCH, etc.) provide specific incident classification for AI-integrity events. Supports customer IR program for AI-related incidents; does not provide general incident response.

Hash chain integrity + Ed25519 signed exports + RFC 3161 timestamps provide cryptographic integrity for AI-decision information. Build SHA stamped on every governance event provides code-level traceability. Verifier CLI checks integrity without vendor access. SI-7 'integrity verification tools' is satisfied for the Permit substrate.

Tier-gated retention (Production 180d, Enterprise 365d), RLS-enforced project isolation, audit-export retention for customer-side archive. Provides the AI-evidence retention substrate; customer establishes overall information management policy beyond AI surface.

Named cryptographic primitives used: SHA-256 (chain), Ed25519 (signatures), AES-256-GCM (provider key encryption), RFC 3161 (timestamping). All NIST-approved or industry-standard primitives. Cryptographic protection is design-level not bolt-on.

RLS isolation at database layer + encrypted provider keys (AES-256-GCM) + R2 checkpoint storage with vendor-managed encryption. Database encryption at rest is the hosting provider's (Supabase / AWS) responsibility under customer's boundary. Permit substrate provides cryptographic integrity (not solely confidentiality) layered on top.

For most B2B SaaS AI workloads that do not process payment card data, PCI DSS is entirely OUT OF SCOPE — these mappings exist for the narrow case where AI processing touches a customer's CDE (e.g., AI-driven fraud detection on transaction data, AI-augmented customer service with payment context). Do not cite PCI mappings broadly for non-CDE AI use cases.

explicit_non_mappings.rationale: Proposed-text trigger 'operation of generative models, such as large language models' was REMOVED in the September 2025 final adopted text. Do not cite as a current trigger. Final scope is limited to ADMT used to REPLACE human decisionmaking for significant decisions (§7150(b)(3)) or training ADMT for those uses or for identity-biological-profiling tech (§7150(b)(6)).

ADMT 'quality of personal information' sub-block (completeness/representativeness/timeliness/validity/accuracy/consistency/reliability) was removed from §7152(a)(2) in the final adopted text. Final §7152(a)(2) only requires identifying categories of personal information processed.

The detailed ADMT evaluation framework with three sub-requirements in proposed (a)(6)(B)(i)–(iii) was reduced to a single line at final §7152(a)(6)(A)(iv): 'Implementing policies, procedures, and training to ensure that the business's ADMT works for the business's purpose and does not unlawfully discriminate based upon protected characteristics.'

SSRF is a transport-layer/application-layer concern handled by network egress controls, URL allowlists, and request-validation libraries in the application. Permit primitive operates at the AI decision boundary and does not control outbound HTTP behavior at the network layer. Customers should address API7 via standard application-security controls.

Security Misconfiguration spans deployment configuration, framework defaults, HTTP headers, error verbosity, and infrastructure hardening — none of which the Permit primitive addresses. Customers should address API8 via standard application-security configuration baselines (e.g., CIS benchmarks).
ASVS v5.0.0 V17 covers WebRTC peer-connection security. Permit primitive is HTTP-API governance and has no WebRTC surface.

Discovery techniques (AML.T0007 Discover AI Artifacts, AML.T0013 Discover AI Model Ontology, etc.) describe adversary recon AFTER access has been obtained. Permit does not detect recon behavior — that is a SOC/EDR responsibility. Permit may provide forensic context post-incident but does not provide preventive or detection evidence for this tactic.
Reconnaissance techniques are pre-engagement adversary behavior outside the Permit primitive's scope. Permit operates inside the customer environment at the AI decision boundary.
